Fraternal (dizygotic) twins arise when two separate eggs are each fertilized by different sperm, so they share about half their DNA like ordinary siblings. Identical (monozygotic) twins arise when a single fertilized egg splits early in development, producing genetically near-identical individuals. Key terms: zygote, dizygotic, monozygotic, ovulation, fertilization, embryo splitting, chorionicity, dichorionic, monochorionic.

Heteropaternal superfecundation: a rare event where two separate eggs released in the same menstrual cycle are fertilized by sperm from different men through separate acts of intercourse, producing fraternal twins with different fathers. Relevant terms include superfecundation, superfetation, heteropaternal superfecundation, dizygotic twins, multiple ovulation, sperm competition, and paternity testing.

Brain tissue lacks nociceptors, the pain-sensing nerve endings found in skin, muscle, and other organs. Pain is therefore not signaled when the brain parenchyma is cut or touched. Relevant terms include nociception, nociceptors, meninges (dura, pia, arachnoid), pain-sensitive structures such as blood vessels, dura mater, and scalp, local anesthesia, conscious (awake) craniotomy, and cortical mapping.

Key concepts: nociceptors and pain-sensitive structures in the head; meninges (dura mater, especially its blood vessels and sensory nerve fibers); the trigeminal nerve and trigeminovascular system; vasodilation and inflammatory mediators; primary versus secondary headache; migraine and vascular theories; central sensitization; and why brain parenchyma lacks nociceptors while the dura and large cranial vessels do not.

Migraine mechanisms: trigeminovascular system, meninges, dura mater, trigeminal nerve, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), cortical spreading depression, aura, vasodilation versus vasoconstriction theory, central sensitization, brainstem and hypothalamus involvement, genetic factors, unresolved causality and ongoing research uncertainty.

Coconut botany: the coconut flower has a tricarpellate (three-carpel) ovary, with three locules. Each carpel corresponds to one of three stigmas and one potential embryo-bearing eye. Germination pores (micropyle/germinal pore area of the endocarp), embryo, plumule and radicle, haustorium, endosperm (coconut meat and liquid), cotyledon, germination valve, seed coat (testa), embryo growth through the soft spot, root emergence, shoot emergence, nutrient absorption, sprouting, fruit dispersal, and the thin membranous tissue covering the pore.

Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid denatures proteins and pepsin cleaves them into smaller polypeptides. In the small intestine, pancreatic proteases such as trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase, plus brush-border peptidases, hydrolyze peptide bonds into free amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides, which are absorbed into the bloodstream.

Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes crown gall via horizontal transfer of T-DNA from its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid into the plant genome. T-DNA carries oncogenes encoding auxin and cytokinin biosynthesis enzymes, causing uncontrolled cell proliferation; opine synthesis supplies nutrients. Plant tumors are non-metastatic, rely on hormone imbalance, and differ from animal cancers, which involve oncogene and tumor suppressor mutations, metastasis, and immune evasion.

Galls form when an organism's tissue grows abnormally in response to an invading agent or stimulus. Key terms: gall-inducing insects (gall wasps, midges, aphids), mites, fungi, bacteria (Agrobacterium, Pseudomonas syringae), and nematodes; wounding; plant hormones (auxin, cytokinin, gibberellin); hyperplasia and hypertrophy; effector molecules; host–parasite interaction; and cecidogenesis, the study of gall formation.

Pheromones are chemical signals released by an organism that trigger behavioral or physiological responses in others of the same species. Ant chemical communication relies on distinct pheromone classes. Trail pheromones, often from the hindgut or Dufour's/poison glands, are volatile or semi-volatile and deposited on the ground. Stereopsis, or stereo vision, lets two eyes estimate depth. Each eye sees a slightly different image because they are horizontally separated, producing binocular disparity. The brain matches corresponding points across the two views and computes their offset, and triangulation over the baseline between the eyes converts that disparity into distance. Binocular disparity shrinks with distance and becomes negligible beyond roughly 10 meters (about 30 feet), so stereopsis gives little depth information for distant objects. Beyond this range the brain relies on monocular cues such as relative size, linear perspective, texture gradient, interposition (occlusion), motion parallax, atmospheric perspective, and familiar size.

Stereopsis and binocular vision: depth from binocular disparity, the retinal offset between two eyes' images, fused by the brain into one 3D percept. Cell membranes are phospholipid bilayers held together mainly by hydrophobic interactions: nonpolar fatty acid tails avoid water and pack together, while polar hydrophilic heads face the aqueous cytosol and extracellular fluid. Van der Waals forces between tails add stability, and the bilayer's self-assembly is driven by the hydrophobic effect, not covalent bonds. Cholesterol, fluidity, and membrane proteins modulate it.
